title: The Somerton Man: Who Was the Stranger With the Secret Pocket?
subject: somerton
description:
Poison, suicide or something else: what do you think happened on Somerton beach? 👇

On 1 December 1948, a well-dressed man was found dead on a beach near Adelaide, with no identification and the labels cut from his clothes. Months later, a hidden pocket gave up two words torn from the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam. This case file follows the suitcase, the nurse, the letters in the book, and the DNA work that put a name to him in 2022.

Sources: Smithsonian Magazine (Mike Dash, 2011; 2022); IEEE Spectrum (2022); Associated Press (July 2022); Wikipedia, "Somerton Man" and its references.

thumbnail.text: TWO WORDS IN A SECRET POCKET

scenes.text: The scrap of paper had been rolled up tight and tucked into a tiny pocket sewn inside the waistband of a dead man's trousers. Earlier examiners had missed it.
It carried two printed words, Tamám Shud. A newspaper reporter recognised them as Persian. Roughly translated, they mean it is finished.
They were the closing words of a famous book of poems, the Rubaiyat of Omar Khayyam, torn from the last page of somebody's copy.
The trousers belonged to a man who had died months earlier on a beach outside Adelaide. Nobody knew his name, and nobody had come to claim him.
He stayed nameless for more than seventy years, at the centre of spy theories, unreadable letters and a nurse who said she had never met him.
Australians came to call him the Somerton Man, and his death became one of the most famous cold cases in the nation's history.
Somerton Park was a quiet seaside suburb about eleven kilometres southwest of central Adelaide. People strolled along the sand below its sea wall.
Around seven o'clock on the evening of the 30th of November, 1948, a jeweller named John Lyons and his wife noticed a man lying on the sand, his head resting against the wall.
His legs were stretched out, feet crossed. As the couple watched, he raised his right arm, then let it drop. They took him for a drunk and walked on.
Half an hour later, a second couple saw him in the same spot. He never once brushed away the mosquitoes, and they assumed he was asleep.
Early the next morning, John Lyons came back to the beach for a swim. The man was still there, slumped against the sea wall, his feet still crossed.
He was cold. A half-smoked cigarette lay on his coat collar, as if it had fallen from his mouth. Police were called.
Detectives soon found that the man had carried almost nothing that could tell them who he was, or where he had come from.
His pockets held an unused train ticket, a bus ticket, a comb, chewing gum and matches. There was no wallet, no money and no identification.
There was also a packet of Army Club cigarettes. Inside it were seven cigarettes of a different, more expensive brand, Kensitas.
His clothes were good quality, but the name tags were gone and nearly every maker's label had been cut away. Unusually for 1948, he wore no hat.
The pathologist put him at forty to forty-five, about five foot eleven, broad-shouldered and fit, with hands that showed no sign of manual work.
His calf muscles were unusually developed and his toes were wedge-shaped. One witness at the inquest wondered if he had been a ballet dancer.
The autopsy found congested organs and a spleen about three times its normal size. His last meal had been a pasty.
Pathologist John Dwyer was sure the death was not natural, yet the government analyst found no trace of poison. “I was astounded that he found nothing,” Dwyer told the inquest.

Cedric Stanton Hicks, of the University of Adelaide, testified that some rare poisons broke down soon after death. He wrote two candidates on paper rather than say them in court: digitalis and strophanthin, both heart drugs.
Six weeks after the death, staff at Adelaide's main railway station handed police a brown suitcase that nobody had come back to collect.
It had been checked into the station cloakroom after eleven on the morning of the 30th of November, the day before the body was found.
Its label was gone too. Inside were a dressing gown, slippers, pyjamas, shaving gear and trousers with sand in the cuffs.
There were tools too: an electrician's screwdriver, a table knife cut down to a short blade, and a stencil brush of a kind used on merchant ships.
A spool of orange waxed thread matched the unusual thread used to mend a pocket in the dead man's trousers.
Three items carried a name: Keane, Kean, and T. Keane. Police searched for a missing T. Keane across the English-speaking world and found nobody.
Months later, pathologist John Cleland re-examined the clothes and found the little pocket sewn inside the trouser waistband. The slip had been there all along.
The words led police to the Rubaiyat. In July 1949, after the story reached the papers, a man from nearby Glenelg brought in a copy with its last page torn.
It had been left in a car, he said. Police called him Ronald Francis to protect his name. The slip matched the torn page.
On the back cover, written in pencil, was a local telephone number. Under ultraviolet light, five lines of faint capital letters appeared beneath it.
The number belonged to a young nurse, Jessica Thomson, who lived about four hundred metres from where the body was found.
She told detectives she did not know the dead man. In 1945, she said, she had given her own Rubaiyat to an army lieutenant in Sydney, Alf Boxall.
Police suspected Boxall, until Sydney detectives found him alive, with his copy of the book and its last page intact.
Shown the plaster cast of the dead man's head, Thomson looked so taken aback, police said, that she seemed about to faint. She turned away.
She never changed her answer. At her request, police kept her name off the record, and books used only pseudonyms. She died in 2007.

scenes.text: The letters proved just as stubborn. Naval intelligence decided they were not a simple cipher, and might be the first letters of lines of verse.
In 1978, defence cryptographers said there were too few symbols to solve. Later statistical studies found they behave like the first letters of English words.
The man was buried at West Terrace Cemetery on the 14th of June, 1949, in dry ground and under concrete, in case he ever had to be exhumed.
Over the years, fresh flowers kept appearing on his grave at irregular intervals. Nobody ever discovered who was bringing them.
The most popular theory was espionage. He died as the Cold War began, his labels cut away, with letters in a book that looked like code.
Boxall had served in a wartime army unit linked to intelligence, which fed the idea. In 1978, he called it “quite a melodramatic thesis”.
Against it, there is no evidence the man had any link to intelligence work, and no hidden message has ever been found in the letters.
The coroner, Thomas Cleland, found that poison had most likely killed him, but could not say whether he took it himself or someone gave it to him.
Cleland also wondered whether the body had been moved there after death. A 1959 police report records a witness who saw a man carrying another man along the beach that night.
Against that, two couples saw a man lying in the same spot hours before he was found, and one of them watched him move his arm.
Some researchers favour suicide: a man who wanted to vanish might cut the labels from his clothes and carry a farewell in his pocket.
In 1994, Victoria's Chief Justice, John Harber Phillips, reviewed the evidence and concluded there seemed little doubt the cause was digitalis. Whether anyone else was involved stayed unanswered.
Every one of these theories needed a name. It would not come until 2022, and it would come from a few strands of hair.
On the 19th of May, 2021, authorities exhumed the body from West Terrace Cemetery for DNA testing. It lay deeper than anyone expected.
Derek Abbott, a University of Adelaide professor, had long been studying hairs caught in the plaster cast made in 1949.
With forensic genealogist Colleen Fitzpatrick, he matched the DNA to distant living relatives and built a family tree of about four thousand people.
One man in that tree had no recorded death. On the 26th of July, 2022, they named him: Carl Webb, known as Charles, an electrical instrument maker from Melbourne.
Webb was born in Footscray, Melbourne, on the 16th of November, 1905. He enjoyed poetry and betting on horses. One of his sisters had married a Thomas Keane.
He married Dorothy Robertson in 1941. They separated, and the last record of him dates from April 1947. By 1951, Dorothy was living in Bute, ninety miles from Adelaide.
Abbott thinks Webb may have come to South Australia looking for her, and that the letters in the book could be a betting list. “This is just us drawing the dots,” he said.
Police called themselves cautiously optimistic, but said more DNA work was needed. The final word on the identification belongs to the state coroner.
Even with a name, the central questions remain open: how he died, why he came to that beach, and whether he ever knew Jessica Thomson.
The paper hidden in his pocket said it is finished. It took nearly seventy-four years for the man who carried it to be given a name.
